title: Migrating right lower quadrant pain in a 65-year-old smoker

source.citation: Chatzelas DA, Atmatzidis SK, Velikoudi MD, Papaziogas V. Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Masquerading as Acute Appendicitis. Cureus. 2025;17(10):e95582.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Acute abdominal pain for six hours, now in the right lower quadrant
presentation.hpi: Sudden abdominal pain that began about 6 h before arrival, first in the epigastrium and soon moving to the right lower quadrant. It is continuous, moderate to severe, and worse with movement, coughing and walking. One episode of vomiting; no other gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, and no constipation, diarrhea or dysuria.

exam: Mild abdominal distension; localized right lower quadrant tenderness with a positive McBurney sign and mild rebound tenderness, without guarding or rigidity
Bowel sounds normal; digital rectal examination unremarkable

imaging.modality: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis (IV contrast, oral gastrografin)
imaging.finding: Previously unknown infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, 70 mm maximum transverse diameter, with a contained retroperitoneal rupture and a large hematoma (about 760 mL) tracking along the right psoas muscle and iliac fascia. Proximal neck 28 mm wide and 19 mm long, angulated about 45°; iliac arteries and access vessels patent, with favorable anatomy.
Bifurcated stent-graft in place; no endoleak

ecg: Sinus rhythm 92/min, normal axis, no acute ST-segment or T-wave changes

diagnosis.primary: Ruptured infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (70 mm) with a contained retroperitoneal hematoma

management: Alvarado score 9/10 suggested appendicitis; contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis was obtained
Vascular surgery consulted immediately; after informed consent, transferred to the hybrid operating room

Emergency EVAR under local anesthesia with bilateral femoral cut-down: 36 mm bifurcated stent-graft from just below the renal arteries to the iliac bifurcations; about 90 min, no intraoperative complications
Transfused 2 units of packed red cells and 2 units of fresh frozen plasma
High-dependency unit for 24 h, then the general ward
Discharged on postoperative day 3 on single antiplatelet therapy
outcome: Uneventful recovery after EVAR; discharged on postoperative day 3 on single antiplatelet therapy. No endoleak on CT angiography at one month; asymptomatic at six months.
teachingPoints: The classic triad of pain, hypotension and a pulsatile mass is present in fewer than half of ruptured AAAs; the report cites up to 42% being first treated as another abdominal condition.
A retroperitoneal hematoma tracking along the psoas can irritate lumbar plexus nerves and mimic appendicitis or ureteric colic, even with a high Alvarado score.
'Stable' vital signs do not exclude rupture: a systolic pressure near 100 mm Hg may be relative hypotension in a treated hypertensive.
In older patients, especially male smokers, with abdominal, flank or back pain, look at the aorta with bedside ultrasound before settling on appendicitis or renal colic.
A contained rupture can bleed again at any time: involve vascular surgery immediately; EVAR is preferred when the anatomy is suitable.

questions.q: Before he is booked for appendicectomy, which bedside test is the most valuable?
questions.extra: Alvarado score 9/10. WBC 18.2 x10³/µL with 81% neutrophils; hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL; CRP 6.1 mg/dL.
options: Point-of-care ultrasound of the abdominal aorta
Repeat Alvarado scoring after IV analgesia
questions.explanation: In a 65-year-old male smoker with hypertension, abdominal pain and a soft blood pressure, a ruptured AAA must be excluded first; bedside ultrasound takes minutes and, as the report notes, is over 95% sensitive for aneurysms larger than 50 mm. The Alvarado score was not designed to exclude a vascular catastrophe, and hematuria does not separate colic from aneurysm.

questions.q: How should his blood pressure of 102/61 mm Hg be interpreted?
options: Reassuring, because the systolic pressure is above 90 mm Hg
An expected effect of his ACE inhibitor alone
A pain-related vagal response needing no action
Possible relative hypotension in a treated hypertensive
questions.explanation: In a known hypertensive, a systolic pressure around 100 mm Hg with a heart rate in the 90s may be relative hypotension and early hemorrhage; 'stable' vital signs do not exclude a contained rupture, which can decompensate suddenly. Attributing it to medication or pain risks false reassurance.

questions.q: What is the preferred definitive management?
questions.extra: CT: 70 mm infrarenal AAA with contained retroperitoneal rupture and a 760 mL hematoma; neck 28 mm wide and 19 mm long, about 45° angulation; iliac and access vessels patent with favorable anatomy.
options: Elective open repair once the hematoma has resorbed
Blood pressure control and repeat CT in 48 hours
questions.explanation: A ruptured AAA needs emergency repair, and ESVS guidelines favor EVAR for rupture when the anatomy is suitable, as it was here (done under local anesthesia). A contained rupture can bleed again at any moment, so delayed repair or observation is not an option.

evidence.quote: A 65-year-old man presented to the emergency department with acute-onset abdominal pain that began approximately six hours prior to admission.
Initially epigastric, the pain quickly migrated to the right lower quadrant (RLQ).
It was continuous, moderate to severe in intensity, and exacerbated by movement, coughing, or walking.
The patient reported a single episode of vomiting but denied other gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms.
There was no history of constipation, diarrhea, or dysuria
He had a 23 pack-year smoking history and a medical history of arterial hypertension and dyslipidemia, managed with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a statin.
On examination, he was fully conscious and oriented.
Vital signs were stable: blood pressure 102/61 mmHg, heart rate 92 bpm, temperature 36.4°C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Abdominal examination revealed mild distension and localized tenderness in the RLQ with a positive McBurney sign. Mild rebound tenderness was present, without guarding or rigidity.
Bowel sounds were normal on auscultation.
digital rectal examination was unremarkable
His hemodynamic stability, absence of a palpable pulsatile mass
SGOT (IU/L) 12 <40 SGPT (IU/L) 18 <41 Urea (mg/dL) 36 0-50 Creatinine (mg/dL) 1.02 0.7-1.2
the Alvarado score was calculated at 9/10, suggesting a high probability of acute appendicitis. Consequently, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed
the CT revealed a previously undiagnosed infrarenal AAA measuring 70 mm in maximum transverse diameter, with evidence of a contained retroperitoneal rupture and a large associated hematoma
with a contained rupture and associated retroperitoneal hematoma (estimated volume: 760 mL)
The contained retroperitoneal hematoma extended along the right psoas muscle and iliac fascia
The proximal aortic neck measured 28 mm in diameter and 19 mm in length, with an angulation of approximately 45°.
Both iliac arteries and access vessels were patent and demonstrated favorable anatomy and wall quality.
Immediately, the vascular surgery team was consulted. After obtaining informed consent, the patient was transferred to the hybrid operating room.
Under local anesthesia and bilateral femoral cut-down, he underwent endovascular AAA repair (EVAR)
using a 36-mm bifurcated self-expanding abdominal aortic
extending from just below the renal arteries to the iliac bifurcations. The procedure lasted approximately 90 minutes and was completed without intraoperative complications.
The patient received two units of packed red blood cells and two units of fresh frozen plasma.
Postoperatively, he was monitored in the high-dependency unit for 24 hours before transfer to the general ward.
His recovery was uneventful, and he was discharged on postoperative day 3 under single antiplatelet therapy.
Follow-up CT angiography (CTA) at one month showed no evidence of endoleak
At six months, the patient remained asymptomatic and continued regular clinical and imaging follow-up.
computed tomography (CT) revealed a large infrarenal AAA with a contained rupture
